blocks.text: I wanted to win a friend, not make an enemy. So I thanked him, gave him the address at Dr. Seward’s, and left. It was dark now, and I was tired and hungry. I got a cup of tea at the Aërated Bread Company and came down to Purfleet on the next train.

I found all the others at home. Mina looked tired and pale, but she made a brave effort to be bright and cheerful. It hurt my heart deeply to think that I had to keep anything from her and make her feel worried and uneasy. Thank God, this will be the last night she has to watch our meetings from the outside. It will be the last night she feels the hurt of our not trusting her with our secrets. It took all my courage to stick to our wise decision to keep her out of our dark, terrible task. Somehow, she seems more ready to accept it. Or else the subject itself seems to have become horrible to her, because whenever anyone mentions it by accident, she actually shivers. I am glad we made our decision in time. With a feeling like this, all the new things we are learning would be torture to her.

I could not tell the others about what I had discovered that day until we were alone. So after dinner, we had a little music to make things look normal, even among ourselves. Then I took Mina to her room and left her to go to bed. The dear girl was more loving with me than ever. She held on to me closely, as if she wanted to keep me there. But there was a lot to talk about, and I came away. Thank God, not telling her things anymore has made no difference between us.

When I came back downstairs, I found all the others gathered around the fire in the study. On the train, I had written my diary up to that point. I simply read it out to them. That was the best way to bring them up to date with what I knew. When I finished, Van Helsing said:

“This has been a great day’s work, friend Jonathan. Without a doubt, we are on the trail of the missing boxes. If we find them all in that house, then our work is near the end. But if some are missing, we must search until we find them. Then we will make our final move and hunt the wretch to his real death.” We all sat in silence for a while. Suddenly, Mr. Morris spoke:
“Say! how are we going to get into that house?”
“We got into the other,” answered Lord Godalming quickly.

“But, Art, this is different. We broke into the house at Carfax, but we had the night and a walled park to protect us. It will be a very different thing to break into a house in Piccadilly, either by day or by night. I admit I don’t see how we are going to get in, unless that man at the agency can find us some kind of key. Maybe we will know when you get his letter in the morning.” Lord Godalming frowned, stood up, and walked around the room. After a little while, he stopped. He turned from one of us to another and said:

“Quincey has good sense. This business of breaking into houses is getting serious. We got away with it once without trouble. But now we have a very hard job ahead of us, unless we can find the Count’s key basket.”

We could not really do anything before morning. It was also at least wise to wait until Lord Godalming heard from Mitchell’s. So we decided not to take any action before breakfast time. For quite a while, we sat and smoked, talking about the matter from different sides. I used the chance to bring this diary right up to this moment. I am very sleepy, and I am going to bed....

Just a line. Mina is sleeping deeply, and her breathing is regular. Her forehead is pulled into little wrinkles, as if she is thinking even in her sleep. She is still too pale, but she does not look as tired and worn out as she did this morning. I hope tomorrow will make all this better. She will be herself at home in Exeter. Oh, but I am sleepy!
